speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, May 2, consideration of Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and Motions No. 23 (Mr. Langdon) (p. 4358) and No. 24 (Mr. Axworthy) (p. 4358) and No. 25 (Mr. Axworthy) (p. 4358).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes one does feel lonely.

Being in the Opposition can be a lonely business. Perhaps some of my colleagues would like to join me-
If 1 am not mistaken, Mr. Speaker, today we are considering the report stage of Bill C-15, and more specifically, a number of amendments that require some serious consideration. The Government, of course, is getting impatient and has imposed closure, thereby restricting speaking time for Members. We shall therefore try to make the best possible use of the time at our disposal, and in fact we shall be trying to improve and make substantial amendments to the legislation before the House today. If I am not mistaken, the motion to be debated now is Motion No. 24, and there are a few comments I would like to make.

This important amendment deals with rental property acquisitions by foreign interests. We are concerned that the kind of blanket exemption currently proposed in the Bill makes it difficult to prevent the occurrence of fiascos such as the Seaway Trust and Greymac affair.

There are no rules to prohibit the kind of transaction we saw in Toronto, where a group of numbered companies, largely financed with foreign capital, spread panic among some
13,000	tenants. Mr. Speaker, I believe we all remember this financial disaster, and I have a few questions. What conditions does the Minister, who is of course again absent from the
debate today .. . what proposals or amendments does the Minister intend to introduce to prevent a recurrence? What sanctions are provided when certain conditions are not observed? Will the Minister go on attracting the big multinationals?

These questions should be answered. They lead us to another important issue, rental housing. Indeed, what has the Government done about rental housing, particularly in a city like Ottawa where the vacancy rate is next to zero? What are the Government's plans in this regard? The Budget did not bring any good news. We saw the Budget of CMHC savaged by the Government. The cash flow of some $30 million was removed from CMHC. We saw no new co-op support and no increased financial support for the housing needs of Canadians.
I am quite concerned that the rental housing market is in particular danger of becoming-

-the prey, as they say in French, of investors whose interests do not really lie in helping Canadians get better housing but in making substantial profits, and it worries me that Bill C-15 does not deal at all with this problem, with a situation that can have disastrous consequences, as we all know.

Indeed, what are the Goverment's plans in this area? What happened to the promise by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) during the last election campaign when he said that co-op housing will continue to have a high priority in the Progressive Conservative policy for housing? 1 ask this in light of major cut-backs in co-op housing in Halifax, Vancouver and Toronto.

I am trying to improve the Bill which you have put on the Order Paper for today. In my view, it is in dire need of improving and if you listen, I am talking about rental properties and how they can be the object of foreign takeovers by foreign capital. Remember the Greymac scandal in Toronto. Hundreds of millions of dollars were artificially inflated in the housing rental market in Toronto, bringing about a catastrophic situation. I take it that the Minister understands what I am talking about now.


Investment Canada Act
I do not know the answers to the questions I have put to the absent Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) regarding rental properties. I hope someone from the Government can give me the answers to those questions because they are important. They must be considered under the purview of this amendment in light of the already stretched housing capacity in our major cities and in light of the blanket exemption currently embodied in the Bill regarding rental property acquisitions. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary what the Government intends to do to prevent rental properties from being acquired by foreign owners who have no interest in the housing markets of today. I put the question in a very serious tone because 1 believe this begs a serious answer.

Mr. Speaker, this starts the final day of clause by clause debate on the Investment Canada Bill. From our point of view, it should not be the final day of clause by clause consideration because there exists within this Bill a great many serious problems and flaws that deserve to be corrected before this Bill goes forward. We had hoped it would have been possible to have sufficient time to talk in detail about each of these particular attempts we have brought forward to improve the character of specific parts of the Bill.
Because we have just this last day been able to consider a whole host of different amendments, for our part we as a Party intend to put up a minimum number of speakers and to try to see to it that it is possible to have at least brief debate on each of the different groupings of amendments before the House for debate.
At the start of today's discussion, I want to point out to Members here in the House and to the public that what we are talking about with this Bill and what we are talking about with the crucial issues of foreign investment is the question of Canadianization of our economy.
We know from public opinion polling that has taken place across the nation that a vast majority, 85 per cent, of Canadians believe in increased Canadianization of our economy. That polling indicates a significant increase in the commitment to Canadianization. The polls in June 1983 indicated only 75 per cent of Canadians at that time felt a strong commitment to Canadianization whereas the most recent polls indicate 85 per cent. This legislation and the attempt we are trying to put forward to improve the Bill focuses on this question of Canadianization.
Are we as a country going to get a greater capacity to put the key parts of our economy into the control of Canadians through the Canadian private sector? Are we going to be able to use the public sector and its regulations to achieve greater Canadian control? Are we going to be able to claim a country for ourselves, for our people and our children in the future that will give the jobs and the economic security so important for all of us?
As this debate goes forward point by point today, I will not be discussing this grand theme of Canadianization, but 1 hope
Members in the House and the people will realize the thrust of the amendments we are bringing forward is to attempt, despite a Bill which has some fatal flaws, some real problems that we cannot correct, to bring forward some positive suggestions for improving the Canadianization of our economy insofar as this Bill can be made to contribute to that goal.
The amendment before us at the moment, Motion No. 23, was moved by myself. Motion No. 23 deals with Part II of the Bill. Within the Bill there is quite a long section which exempts certain important categories of enterprise from review, despite the fact that the Bill provides for some review. As Hon. Members know, it provides for the review of acquisitions of companies which have over $5 million in assets, are Canadian controlled and are taken over by foreign companies. Within the attempt to maintain at least some kind of review process, certain exemptions are set out, some of which frankly make sense, but a number of which do not make sense.
[DOT] (MI5)
For the benefit of Hon. Members, I point to the specific clause to which Motion No. 23 applies, subclause (c) on page 6 which indicates that the acquisition of control of a Canadian business is exempt from review in connection with the realization of security granted for a loan or other financial assistance.
Quite recently there was a case in Smiths Falls, Ontario, concerning a small company called R-J Stamping which employed a significant number of people. That company was forced into bankruptcy and as a result, its physical assets were sold off to a foreign purchaser. The jobs which existed within that community, and of course the potential for future jobs, disappeared as the physical assets were literally shipped out of the country. In that particular case, the local provincial Member, who happens to be a Conservative, raised serious questions about it with the Premier of Ontario, the Hon. Frank Miller. Mr. Miller took this case very seriously, if not others, perhaps because it was the middle of an election campaign. He probed the case of this particular company and indicated that it should not be possible for its physical assets simply to be sold out of the country without any review process. Mr. Miller, as Premier of Ontario, said: "Let's get the Foreign Investment Review Agency to look at this case".
Frank Miller said that!
He said that, believe it or not.
Unbelievable.

Unfortunately Mr. Miller did not realize that F1RA, as it had been put in place, had as one of its weaknesses the fact that it did not cover such cases as this, where a company went bankrupt and its assets were then sold off to foreigners.
Being a loyal citizen of Ontario, and seeing that the Premier of my province wanted action taken on this particular gap in our capacity to review foreign takeovers, I moved this motion. Unfortunately it was voted down, unbelievably, in committee by members of the Conservative Party, the very Party which


Frank Miller represents. Once more 1 bring this case before the House of Commons in the hope that common sense will somehow prevail, in the hope that government Members sitting here today will recognize that this amendment is not meant to be frustrating to this Bill. It is not meant to be somehow destructive, but rather is an amendment which aims simply to fill a gap which exists in the legislation. It is a gap which we have discovered also existed in the previous legislation and, frankly, deserves to be corrected. I strongly urge government Members to support Motion No. 23 because it will have the effect of filling a gap which even the Premier of Ontario has recognized needs to be filled.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to address Bill C-15 with respect to Investment Canada today. Recognizing that what is being proposed here is that increased capital and technology will benefit Canada and that the purpose of the Bill is to encourage investment in Canada by Canadians and non-Canadians, I rise to support such an activity, and I do so with pride.
If Bill C-15 achieves the two fundamental objectives of more economic growth and more employment opportunities, we will have to recognize the problems that existed with FIR A. I have taken the opportunity to ask my constituents how they feel about foreign investment in Canada and if they feel that it helps create jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. We are presently dealing with Motions Nos. 23, 24 and 25. I think the Hon. Member should address the subject matter of those particular amendments.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) is correct. I am sure the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) will act accordingly.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will get to that, as the Hon. Member will see if he has any patience. The Hon. Member who spoke previously referred to polls which indicate what he felt the people of the country wanted. The results of a recent poll just came out. I found it interesting to note that that poll indicated that only a bare minimum of New Democrat voters wanted foreign investment in Canada. That is all part of this Bill. Let me address that very phrase.
There is an NDP Government in Manitoba right now. Although Members of the NDP state philosophically that they are not in favour of any foreign investment in Canada and that businesses in Canada must be totally Canadian owned, the NDP Government in Manitoba will put its arms around foreign companies, give them a kiss, make love to them and then, when they make a profit, call them corporate welfare bums. That is the attitude of the NDP Government.
The Hon. Member proposes changes, but they are not changes that will benefit this Bill. In fact, the changes go to the very heart of what they feel, which is that foreign investment in any form is not the greatest and is not highly
Investment Canada Act
desirable. He is never happy with that. When we encourage investment being brought into the country, that stops us from importing goods. It stops us from importing goods which could be manufactured here in Canada. That will certainly help our entire situation. In effect, we would be using our natural resources right here. We would be using Canadian labour and gain from the resources and technologies brought in by foreign companies. Surely the Hon. Member cannot be opposed to that.
The Hon. Member mentioned that some 80 per cent of the population was in favour of Canadianization. If a product is manufactured here in Canada, then is that not Canadianization of that product? Is that not better than importing goods made completely in some other country? The Hon. Member suggests we wait until a Canadian can put a company in place which can perform the research and development with regard to the production of a product. He would allow a limited amount of foreign investment while Canadianizing the other part. I am sorry to say we probably would not have 90 per cent of the products we have here in Canada if we had to wait for them to be developed in this country. As a matter of fact, the country is comprised of people who come from many countries and who brought with them their ideas and technology.
If the Hon. Member wishes to point out the results of a recent poll in support of his point of view, then I suggest we must look to all areas of investment. We must consider foreign capital which comes into the country. We must take into consideration FIRA. Those in favour of FIRA claim a success rate in that regard. However, if you were to talk to international people from places such as New York and Tokyo, you would find they did not want to come here because they did not want to deal with FIRA. They did not want to deal with the types of laws which were in place.
There are no simple solutions. However, some of the amendments have to be addressed. I must ask whether or not they have been well thought out. Are those who propose the amendments aware of the ramifications? Is it just a matter of these people sitting back and dreaming? All too often Oppostion Members dream these amendments up because they hate the fact we have changed something which they put in place. Why do they not stand up and admit that? That would give some honesty to the system.
The Hon. Member recommends a change to a specific clause. That is not the total solution. The change has not been well thought out. We must take into consideration the manufacture of Canadian products with Canadian raw materials through the use of foreign research and development. That is the idea here.
In my riding alone, as a result of FIRA, three large investment groups were turned away because there was too much negativism involved in the whole system. There was just too much red tape to go through. Those three groups would have been in place in my riding had it not been for FIRA. There


Investment Canada Act
could be an additional 700 jobs in my riding now had Investment Canada been in place then as it has been proposed today.
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. Would it be possible for the Hon. Member to use the last minute of his 10 to deal with the subject of debate?

speechtext: I regret to inform the Hon. Member that that is not a point of order. Resuming debate. I will recognize the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

Mr. Speaker, as you said, the remarks which were made by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) did not constitute a point of order, but he did make a very interesting point. Perhaps Tory Members who failed to speak on the main motion could remember that. Perhaps Tory Members should read the motions which the House is debating before making speeches. I am sure it would be most constructive if you brought that to their attention, Mr. Speaker.
1 found it interesting that the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) challenged Parliament's right to amend Government legislation. That shows the respect for democracy which Tories have. They are challenging the fundamental right of Parliament to amend Government legislation. I see an Hon. Member opposite who is laughing. Some day in the future when factories close down in his riding because of this legislation and his voters knock on his door to ask him why he failed to amend and improve the legislation, they will know what he did.
We are discussing Motions Nos. 23, 24 and 25. With respect to Motion No. 25, we are proposing an improvement in the Bill which is a form of preventive medicine. We want to ensure that insurance companies are included in the notification and possibly in the review process of foreign acquisitions. We know that increasingly the ownership questions related to large pools of capital are accumulated by major financial institutions. In that case, there appears to be a loophole for foreign insurance companies. I had hoped that the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake would have referred to that. Perhaps he is not concerned about that issue. He is only concerned about challenging Parliament's right to amend Government Bills.
It should be remembered that opposition Members have never stated they were against foreign investment. The Opposition wants what is best for Canadians. The Tories have no right to stop us from presenting motions which will improve the legislation. Ronnie and his nephew, Brian, had a little duet in Quebec City.
What is the amendment?

When the Government and its Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) failed to put a stop on countervail duties in the United States, where were Tory Members? Why were they not acting in the best interests of Canadians? Why did they not bring forward amendments such as Motion No. 25 in order to ensure that the Bill would be better for all Canadians?
I notice an Hon. Member opposite who was once a Liberal. He too lost his way. Perhaps, he could find the energy to speak on the Bill. Perhaps he could tell the Prime Minister not to make the statements which were reported in Fortune magazine when he spoke against Canadians and the workers of the country. In the article he said:


Who wants to buy it? What is there so compellingly attractive about Canada that causes us to think that anybody is going to rush in simply because somebody says, "I'd like to do business with you." We do not have a very good track record. Our products have not been of the highest quality. Our deliveries have been lacking in reliability. Our expertise has been in large measure borrowed. Our technology has been purchased. What the hell makes us so special?
Those are the comments of the Conservative Prime Minister. 1 wish some of his back-benchers would stand and speak in favour of the positive amendments which are being presented today in order to ensure that we will have a fair share of Canadianization, and that the Bill and the amendments which have been proposed will ensure that in the future we will not see large foreign takeovers. Obviously, that will happen if the Bill is passed without amendments. All Conservative members opposite and the book-ends and surfers on this side of the House should remember that and stop thinking that they are only here for a short time. They are making the best of it. They are not here for a long time, they are here for a short time, but a good time. Nevertheless, they should stand in the House and speak on behalf of their voters. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais) should state clearly that he is against the countervail duties of the United States. He should take the opportunity to speak about Canadianization.

He does get that way whenever he feels threatened. It's not his fault. If I were a Tory, I would be embarrassed right now as well. We were discussing Amendments Nos. 23, 24 and 25 to this Bill, Mr. Speaker.
Why don't you discuss them?

I've been discussing them all along, Mr. Speaker, and I challenge the Hon. Member to say, for instance, whether he is in favour of the very excellent real estate amendments under Motion No. 23 and whether he thinks, as we do, that Motion No. 25 would indeed act as preventative medicine in ensuring that insurance companies be included in the notification process? Members of the Opposition have been speaking to those amendments. Perhaps we should speak a little more slowly so that the Conservatives could understand. 1 will try to do that in future just to ensure that they keep up to our train of thought.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that Motion No. 25 should be adopted by this House because it would vastly improve the proposed legislation. Actually, the only way to amend this Bill would be for the Government to abandon it forthwith. However, if the Government does not give up its proposed legislation in favour of what we had before, the second best option is for the Government to adopt the amendments proposed by the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, 1 intend to speak to these amendments and I invite all Hon. Members of the Conservative Party to do so, particularly those representing urban ridings, such as the City of Toronto-and it is unfortunate that there are a number of Hon. Members from Toronto who are not here-and the Cities of Vancouver, Montreal, Halifax, Edmonton, Calgary and all of those areas where tenants rely on the protection of government to ensure that their particular stability is not threatened.
Some Hon. Members may not remember that I was in the Ontario Legislature at the time of the famous "flip" deal when more than 10,000 apartment units in the City of Toronto changed hands. Their rental value would have doubled, tripled and, in some cases, quadrupled, as a direct result of a transaction which would have been, under the current law, deemed to


Investment Canada Act
be illegal. Without these amendments, the Government is saying that any real estate sale to a foreign company will not be subject to review by Investment Canada. Those 20,000 tenants who live at the corner of Yonge and Eglinton in the City of Toronto, who received protection from the Government at the time of that flip-flop deal-and people like Howard Brown were involved with the tenants' organizations in their fight against those particular increases-will now have no protection. This Government has failed to protect tenants by omitting to include the amendments which have been proposed by both Opposition Parties.
I would like to ask those Hon. Members from the urban centres, and particularly those from the City of Toronto, to talk about how they are going to fight for tenants' rights. They have a chance with this amendment to put their money where their mouths are. Any Hon. Member who supports this government's move to remove this real estate protection from consideration has, in fact, abdicated his or her responsibility to the tenants in his or her riding. I ask all Hon. Members of the Government to take a look at the amendment to see what is involved because this particular amendment will ensure that foreign investment in Canadian real estate is subject to review by Investment Canada.
Not only has this Government said that all investment under $5 million will no longer be subject to review, but that any investment in Canadian real estate over $5 million, will not be subject to review. The particular amendment which we are proposing would in fact ensure that at the very least the rather flimsy review provisions of Investment Canada of transactions over $5 million would include the real estate market.
We are not talking simply about company transactions as has happened recently with the Nabisco deal. What we are talking about is the kind of direct cause and effect relationship which a purchase of Canadian real estate can have not only on the Canadian stock market and the Canadian investment community, but on Canadian tenants. I remind those Hon. Members from the City of Toronto who have failed to speak up on this very important issue of a real estate deal which turned sour. It was a trust fiasco, according to the Financial Times of Canada, dating back to January 31, 1983. Right from the start it was a deal of daunting complexity punctuated with pure theatre of the absurd. Witness, for example, the closing on the sale of 10,931 Toronto apartment units which formed the core of the most celebrated real estate deal in Canadian history. The apartments were to be flipped through several hands from Cadillac Fairview Corporation Limited to a series of numbered companies later said to be controlled by Saudi-Arabian investors. That particular celebrated flip of more than 10,000 apartment units would have obviously impacted directly on the lives of the people in the City of Toronto.
It was as a result of the combined efforts of the Foreign Investment Review Agency and provincial government legislation that we were able to ensure that the cost pass through, which was to have been passed on to tenants and which would have resulted in increases of 300 per cent, 400 per cent, 500
per cent and 600 per cent in direct rental charges, was disallowed. Those tenants were saved from having to pay for the flip-flop deal which was the most celebrated deal in Canadian real estate history.
I hope that those Hon. Members who are seeking re-election in the City of Toronto, in the City of Vancouver, which has one of the lowest vacancy rates in Canada, and in the City of Halifax where the rental housing situation has reached crisis proportions, will realize that in defeating this amendment they will be placing themselves in the position of having to go to their constituents in the next election campaign and saying to them, "We had a chance to protect you or to even offer the minimal $5 million protection under Investment Canada, but we turned our backs because we are not interested in protecting tenants". Instead the Conservatives have said, "Come and invest in Canada. You can buy up millions upon millions of dollars worth of Canadian real estate without being subject to any kind of notification analysis or review by the Government of Canada". The particular decision by this Government to wash its hands of concern for tenants, as it has so clearly indicated by exempting real estate specifically from the provisions for the $5 million review, is just another indication of how this Government is prepared to let those people who are in the least position to protect themselves hang out to dry.
We heard the Government promise to protect the housing situation in Canada. We heard the government promises to senior citizens. Of the tens of thousands of apartment dwellers in the City of Toronto and the thousands in the City of Hamilton a great proportion are senior citizens. Those are the same people from whom the Government is taking $30 a month and calling it chicken feed. The Government says that it can take $30 a month from the senior citizens because they do not care.
Order.

Perhaps the Member does not see the relevance.
I am talking about a government exemption of real estate purchases by foreign companies which will directly impact upon the cost of rental for people living in highly populated urban areas, the majority of whom are single and living alone, many elderly widows, who are extremely concerned about the negative impact of the Government's initiatives on senior citizens' pensions. Those same people will now be faced with a further potential rent increase as a direct result of the Government's failure to approve the amendment that we have suggested with respect to real estate.
Nonsense.

The Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) says "nonsense". I urge the Member for Mississauga South to speak on this issue because Mississauga happens to be one of the largest growing tenant areas in Canada. If the Member were truly representing his constituents, he would say that real estate, as any other investment, is an investment in


Canada and subject to review under the Canada Investment Act or by the Canadian Government. In fact, if the Member for Mississauga South had read the amendment, he would have been aware that we are attempting to allow the Government the same possibility of review that it had on the Player's flip-flop apartment takeover. Conservatives in the City of Toronto were scurrying on side on that issue. They realized that rental increases of 100 per cent, 200 per cent, 300 per cent, and 400 per cent for senior citizens in those areas was unconscionable.
The Government is going to wash its hands of the whole issue by telling the world that Canada is open for business, to come in and buy up our apartment blocks by the hundreds and thousands and the purchases will not even be subject to notification, let alone review. The cost pass through of the flip of 10,000 apartments in the City of Toronto was prevented because of Liberal legislation in the Federal Investment Review Agency. Such cost pass throughs will be paid directly on the backs of tenants.
I am sorry if the Member for Mississauga South does not want to speak for his constituents. I am sorry that Government Members have not taken the time to read this amendment. If they had done so, they would not be so quick to tell their constituents that they are fighting on behalf of poor people.

The exemption in Bill C-15, which is addressed in Motion No. 23, relates to security granted for a loan. Members have not yet spoken about this. It would be instructive for Canadians to learn more about what the unholiest alliance in Canadian history, the Liberals and New Democrats, is purporting that the Government should consider.
The motion deals with the deletion of certain lines and clauses in the Bill to the effect that the exemption for acquisitions resulting from the realization of security granted for a loan would not be dealt with. The intent of Bill C-15 is that non Canadians should be able to enforce the security provisions of a loan agreement and acquire control of a Canadian business without being subject to the notification provisions if a Canadian business has sought a loan from a non-Canadian Financial institution and signed a loan agreement such as a Canadian would sign with a local bank. The Liberals and New Democrats are saying that they want the access to capital by small, medium, and large Canadian companies limited. This motion would restrict the security of the person or institution lending the money. Who would willingly lend money without a guarantee of security? This motion makes that subject to notification and frightens lenders about doing business in Canada.


Investment Canada Act
Bill C-15 is trying to address the problem of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. Investment Canada is trying to deal with that problem by restoring confidence. Such motions as these moved by the New Democratic Party take away confidence. They tell non-Canadian lenders that they will be subject to all sorts of notification in order to enforce a security agreement in a loan. That does not inspire confidence.
Earlier some of my colleagues were citing statistics and figures. Most important when we look at the motions, the average Canadian recognizes that when we do not accept those motions and the frivolous measures being brought in by the Opposition, they can have confidence in us. It is investment confidence that Canadians see in the Government, Members of the Cabinet and the overwhelming number of Conservative Members of Parliament who outnumber the dwindling numbers in the Opposition ranks every day.
Motion No. 23 shows what the unholy NDP-Liberal alliance is doing once again to small, medium and large Canadian businesses that simply want to turn to a non-Canadian lender for some capital so that they may create jobs and create confidence in our economy.

Mr. Speaker, as I said before, it is absolutely vital that Canadians realize the Government is taking a new and open attitude toward foreign investment, an attitude that can be felt among all Government Members here in the House and across the country. If we look at the recent Budget, the cutbacks in old age pensions will be devastating. If we have rental accommodation going up dramatically, how will senior citizens be able to find accommodation? Practically every senior citizen has to look at the prospect of $200 less in purchasing power next year. If they are receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement, that will be reduced as well. These people are living at or below the poverty line.
I think Government Members would be sympathetic to anything that would benefit our senior citizens. In the projection of the cut-backs in old age pensions over four or five years, we are talking of some $1,500 according to a recent study done by the Canadian Press. We have to be concerned about our senior citizens.
When a deal like the Seaway Trust Greymac flip goes bad, it not only affects housing accommodation, but it affects all kinds of other businesses and properties throughout the country that are held by the institutions as well as the individuals involved. In my own constituency, there is a very important recreational area, a ski hill development, which was thrown into turmoil and still has difficulties because of that takeover problem. I think Motion No. 24 would be very acceptable to Government Members who would be concerned about those kinds of takeovers. There are many actions in the Budget which relate in a similar way. I see the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has left. He is the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. That committee conducted an excellent study of the farm debt crisis facing some 40,000 young farmers across the country. That committee made an excellent report.


calling upon the Government to establish a rescheduling of farm debt and to institute a program of medium term loans at 8 per cent interest up to $300,000 which it was estimated would benefit some 14,000 of the 40,000 farmers facing serious financial difficulties this coming year.
Although the committee made those recommendations to the Government and to the House in its report, when the Budget came down, lo and behold, there was no decision by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to do anything about them. This is viewed by the agricultural community as a total abandonment of the Government's responsibility in this regard. In southwestern Ontario, as Canadian farmers go out of business, face foreclosure or go into bankruptcy, farm after farm is being bought up by foreign interests from Europe. If those interests settled down and lived on the land, that would be one thing, but often the houses and barns are simply razed and the land is put up for rental. The whole community life is destroyed by such action.
We see a Government hell bent on foreign investment at any price, regardless of whether there are any benefits for Canada. At the same time, it exacerbates this by completely abandoning its traditional role in agricultural financing. We really have a double whammy in that regard.
When we look at the Western Accord and at the budget Bills which were introduced relating to foreign investment, we see that multinational oil companies-and this is according to an estimate by Informetrica-over the next five years will actually be given $10.9 billion. I suppose the sad part is that it does not come from someone strange; it comes from Caandian taxpayers-little pensioners who are having trouble financing their rental accommodations will each have to give up $100 per year, the average family of four will have to pay some $400 extra per year, and people who have to commute in northern areas will have to pay an extra two cents per litre or nine cents per gallon starting in early September. What is this all for?
1 read a report this week which indicated that Trilogy Resource Corporation of Calgary, a junior Canadian company producing only 800 barrels per day, was concerned about all the riches which were showered on large multinationals like Imperial and so on, and that there would be massive takeovers as a result of the budget Bills and the Western Accord. Let us look at the financial picture of Imperial. Its 1984 profits over 1983 were $533 million. I speak about this because of the whole attitude of the Government in this Bill, in the amendments, and in the discussions on the amendments, that all foreign takeovers and all foreign investment are good, without regard to Canadian ownership. I would think the Government would want to strengthen its position.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) said in a speech in Inuvik that the policy of the Tory Government of Canada was greater Canadian ownership. How do we square that with this Bill which just leaves everything wide open for foreign takeovers below $5 million? We are
Investment Canada Act
dealing with a Government which seems to be talking out of both sides of its mouth. Supposedly it wants greater benefits for Canada, but as far as screening companies and investment groups from West Germany, Austria and Europe in general coming in to take over farms-and they are taking over dozens of them in southwestern Ontario-no questions are asked, regardless of whether they raze the buildings, rent out the land and completely destroy community life. As long as the cash is there, it does not seem to matter. That is the same with the Western Accord. Small Canadian oil companies are being led to the slaughter and will be taken over by large multinationals which will pick up $800 million in existing oil reserves.

The confidence in this Government is badly shaken, not only by the Budget but by the Bill which we are debating today.

Mr. Speaker, I shall avoid paying further compliments to Conservative Members as they do not seem to be in the mood to accept them this morning.
We have before us a group of amendments that attempt to improve in this case in relatively minor ways the Investment Canada Bill. 1 shall speak specifically with respect to Motion No. 27. The clause that we are suggesting should be amended is one which deals with the question of notification.
For Hon. Members who have not followed this debate in detail, I would make the introductory point to Hon. Members who are present that this Bill identifies within it three categories of enterprises. The first category of enterprises comprises take-overs by foreign companies of Canadian companies with assets of at least $5 million. For that particular category of enterprises, there must be notification and there must be review of that take-over.
There is a second category of enterprises which is composed of foreign companies entering this country to establish new businesses. Under the present Bill, each new business established through this kind of foreign entry must notify Investment Canada that a new business has been established. However, there is a third category of enterprises within this Bill comprising the set of enterprises which are subject to special consideration because they have an impact on the cultural heritage and national identity of Canada.
With respect to the third category of enterprises, it is possible, if the Minister wishes to do so and subject to certain regulations that are set out by the Governor in Council, for a firm to be subject to review despite the fact that that firm may have assets of less than $5 million being taken over and despite the fact that it might be a new business which is being established. In short, this is a category of enterprises for which it may very well be possible for a review to take place as well as for a notification to be required.
The way this particular part of the Bill is set up suggests that certain enterprises are subject only to notification. According to this part of the Bill, if a firm is subject to notification, it is not subject to review as these are two different categories of firms.
Our amendment makes it clear that there is the possibility that an investment that is being made to establish a new Canadian business may be subject to review even though it is included in the category of businesses subject to notification. The reason for that is the existence of that special clause which deals with cultural heritage and national identity. In a very real sense, we are talking about a technical amendment that would make the Bill itself consistent.
1 would refer Hon. Members to Clause 11, Subclause (b) of Bill C-15. Clause 11 presently reads:
The following investments by non-Canadians are subject to notification under this Part:
(b) an investment to acquire control of a Canadian business in any manner
described in subsection 28(1), unless the investment is reviewable pursuant to
section 14.
If the business is reviewable, it will then be subject to review and not notification. However, Subclause (a) of Clause 11 suggests that a business subject only to notification is:
(a) an investment to establish a new Canadian business;-
As I have indicated, it is possible under this Bill for a new Canadian business being established by a foreign firm to be subject as well to review. That is why we have moved an amendment in Motion No. 27 that will simply change Subclause (a) so that it will read:


(a) an investment to establish a new Canadian business unless it is reviewable under Part IV;-
This Motion simply clears up what could be a potential conflict that could emerge when the Bill becomes an Act.
Our amendment simply provides that when there are cases in which the Government wishes to use its cultural heritage and national identity clause, it will be possible to use that clause with respect to new investments in Canada by nonCanadian firms. That is the technicality of the amendment. The substance that lies beneath the technicality is that the operative part of this Bill which is very important to the future is the clause that permits review to take place in cases where we have a potential threat to the cultural heritage or national identity of Canada. It is a part of the Bill which Conservative Ministers have been quite anxious to highlight in the public debates which have taken place.
In order for that particular clause to be operative, I would argue that an amendment must be accepted with respect to the clause which permits exceptions to exist, in which new businesses coming in from the outside will be subject to review, not just to notification. If that is not included, then there is a potential conflict between this clause and the clause in the Bill which permits the Government to designate, for review, cases in which cultural heritage and national identity considerations are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, now that Parliament is once again working as it should and we are into a period of constructive examination of a number of important amendments-and perhaps the new atmosphere is a direct result of not having the esteemed Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) with us-I hope that the new aura of an open-minded and constructive approach will continue on the part of the Government. The amendments which we have introduced are an attempt to improve the legislation and not in any way to interrupt or disagree with the principles of it. Again, the amendments are based upon the proposals and representations which were made at committee hearings.
Motion No. 30 is a very important amendment. It deals with a problem which we detected in the legislation, whereby the proposed foreign investor has the right not to provide notification until 30 days after the fact. In the amendment, we are saying that there should be a requirement of notification before implementation of a particular investment, so that the Government would not be put in a position of having to review an investment-and at times be forced to disagree with it and reject it-and force a major divestiture on the part of the investor.
Under the present legislation, investors can indicate their acquisitions or takeovers, acquire the properties and notify after the fact.
As the Chamber of Commerce pointed out, that would
result in a forced fire sale of a number of acquisitions if the
Investment Canada Act
Government were to decide that the investments should not be approved. Therefore, a number of companies would be faced with a degree of uncertainty. In the amendment, we are attempting to deal with what was probably an oversight, lack of experience, judgment or analysis on the part of the persons who drafted the legislation or the Minister. For the sake of the business community, according to all the proposals and presentations which have been made by the Government, it wants to provide more flexibility and an easier sense of procedure. This particular clause forces the business community to face the potential awkwardness of having to divest itself of a holding after that holding has already been acquired. Therefore, Motion No. 30 seeks the requirement that notification be given up to one day before implementation, so that the agency would have the right to provide a signal to the company and not have to wait for a post hoc situation to occur.
Government Members who are concerned and interested in ensuring that the legislation is simplified should carefully examine the amendment and realize that it meets one of the major objections which was brought before the committee by members of the business community. I do not know why the Minister ignored that representation. He has said that he believes in consultation. However, in this particular case he ignored it. We are proposing the amendment to respond to what we believe is the general interest which has been put forward by the Government. It will provide a review procedure which is simple and easy to understand. It will not carry with it any awkwardness or the potential problems of post hoc decisions which would force major fire sale investitures.
Motion No. 67 refers to a matter which is important to the legislation. The Government has indicated very clearly that there should be a special set-aside provision for cultural industries. It recognizes that those industries are a part of the area of foreign investment which have particular sensitivities and require special examination. If that is the case, then sufficient time should be given to fully examine the full range of potential problems. Therefore, in the amendment we have proposed that an extra 15 days be allotted for the review of areas dealing with the cultural or national identity parts of foreign investment takeovers or acquisitions. The reason for the extended time, and it is not a great amount of time, is to take note of the requirement that, in complicated areas such as book publishing, there should be sufficient time for the necessary consultation, and particularly in areas where there could be potential Canadian buyers.
We introduced an earlier amendment which was rejected by the Government. It proposed that the Minister be responsible, in cases concerning cultural industries, to seek out alternative Canadian buyers for industries such as book publishing, records and electronics. The Government rejected that amendment. However, it would seem that the purpose of Investment Canada is to secure Canadian investment. That should be its primary objective. Therefore, that amendment would only seem reasonable when there is a proposed takeover by a foreign company.


There are a number of such takeovers presently on the books. For example, the Minister has taken over six months to examine the Prentice-Hall takeover. However, under this legislation, he said that it would be done within 30 days. Well, if he cannot conclude his examination of Prentice-Hall within six months, surely some extra time should be allowed.
I do not want to prejudge the motivation of the Minister. Perhaps taking six months is a good thing. If I were the Minister, I would have decided within 30 days that the Prentice-Hall takeover made absolutely no sense, because Gulf and Western already have a substantial number of publishing holdings in Canada. However, it is already taking an exorbitant amount of time for key acquisitions which are on the table. Therefore, it would seem only logical that the same kind of consideration be accorded to this amendment which would allow additional time for consideration of investments by foreigners in the cultural area. It is a part of our society which we cannot afford to deal with in an offhand manner.
I have heard the Minister say that FIRA applications should be passed without much review or examination. Certainly, we have seen in the months since the Government has come to power that there has not been one rejection of a FIRA application. Surely if the legislation denotes a consideration for cultural industries, then sufficient time should be allocated to ensure that all the questions pertaining to the acquisition are properly examined, and, most important, that the Minister has sufficient time to make arrangements for alternative buyers in the Canadian market-place.
That is the primary purpose of the amendment. We hope, as we saw in the last round of considerations, that government Members will again show good judgment and agree to what is obviously a very helpful amendment to their cause.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order in an effort to be sure that the record of this morning's proceedings will show what actually took place. I would like to ask the House and the Table to take a look at what happened. I am referring to the fact that earlier today, Motions Nos. 23, 24 and 25 were grouped for debate and that debate took place in the House with Members from both sides of the Chamber.
A member of the Official Opposition asked if we had any further speakers on the particular motion and we agreed that in the spirit of co-operation, so that members of the Official Opposition could refresh their list, we would stand our speakers. At that point, I believe the record will show that the Deputy Speaker called for the vote on Motion No. 23.
At the start of the calling for the vote, the Deputy Speaker did not point out-and I am not sure whether he should or should not have, as 1 think it is for the Chair to decide-that the votes on Motions Nos. 23, 24 and 25 would be taken separately. Therefore, I believe the record will show that the Deputy Speaker called the vote on Motion No. 23 and asked: "Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?" I believe the record will show that on Motion No. 23 yeas and nays were recorded. The Deputy Speaker then said: "All those in favour of the motion will please say yea." I believe the record will show that there were yeas. The Deputy Speaker then said: "All those opposed will please say nay." I believe the record will show that Hon. Members said nay. It is also my
belief that five members of the Opposition stood when the Deputy Speaker said: "In my opinion, the nays have it." As is their right, members of the Opposition stood to formally request a recorded vote. Then, pursuant to Standing Order 79(11), the Deputy Speaker said: "A recorded division on the proposed motion stands deferred." I am not sure whether he said "motion" or "motions", but, the point is that when the Deputy Speaker moved to Motion No. 24, 1 believe the record will show that he said: "Mr. Axworthy moved that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be amended in Clause 10 by striking out lines 43 to 48 at page 6. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?" I believe at that point opposition Members said yea, quite naturally. I know, and I can only speak for myself in the House, that I definitely said nay. Sitting in my place, I said nay. I am not sure the record will show that. There are records which the Chair will have the opportunity to examine; there is Hansard and there is the video tape of the proceedings. I am sure that the Chair, in the interest of fairness and in the interest of deciding what actually took place, with precedents in mind, will examine all of those.
Point number one of my point of order is that I believe the video tape records will show, display-in other words, Mr. Speaker, you will hear it-that there were yeas and nays. I realize that is an imperfect way of doing it, but I believe it can be drawn, from what I had an opportunity to hear earlier, that my nay was part of that confusion. 1 must admit that my hearing is biased on that point.
The second point of the point of order is that I believe the record will show that at no time did the Deputy Speaker say, as he did when he was on Motion No. 23; "In my opinion, the yeas have it." I believe, at the point at which the vote is called, that it is up to the Chair to declare the motion won or lost. I believe the record will show that at that point he did not declare the motion to be won or lost, but moved on to Motion No. 25. I submit that the Chair is the person in the House who decides whether motions have been won or lost. The only way in which he can express that opinion is to say it. In other words, I believe if the record is examined it will show that some Members agreed and then it will show that the Deputy Speaker moved on to Motion No. 25, without formally declaring the previous motion won or lost.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that until that declaration is made, the motion is in a hiatus. In other words, it has not been won, it has not been lost, and it is up to the Chair to declare whether it has been won or lost. If the Chair makes that declaration at the time of the vote-and if the Chair declares that the vote was won by the Opposition, then that's fair ball- then we should have the opportunity, as the Government, just as the Opposition did on the first motion, to stand our five Members. Certainly, we had five Members in the House. We should have had the opportunity to stand our five Members and request a recorded division on the vote. That did not happen. I suggest that is the third thing which should have happened. We should have had that opportunity.


In review, there are three things which 1 would ask the Chair to consider: one, whether the yeas and nays were properly heard and recorded; two, whether the Deputy Speaker ever officially declared the motion won or lost, and three, whether Members of the House on all sides had that democratic opportunity to have five Members stand and request an official recorded division of the vote.
1 appreciate that things happen quickly in the House. There have been many, many opportunities when we, as the Government, have given the Opposition the benefit of the doubt in the interest of doing what the majority of Members of the House want done. I suggest that in the future there will be those opportunities. That is what this place is all about. They can argue, "Sorry, Mr. Simcoe North; sorry, Mr. Lewis; sorry. Government, we tricked you because something went by." That is not the point of this place.
You fumbled the ball, that's the problem. Why not kick it in the end zone now?

speechtext: I admit I don't know all the rules. Would the person who knows all the rules please stand-other than yourself, Sir? I would ask the honorary member at the table if he does not agree that what this place is really all about is that what Hon. Members want done, properly gets done in accordance with the rules, and not only the rules of the House but the rules of fair play. I would ask the Chair and the Table Officers to examine whether in fact my three points within the point of order have validity and then I would put it to the test of Hon. speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) stood in his place and said, "I said 'nay' ". I know that there are other Hon. Members in this House who are prepared to say that they said "nay". Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, the Government House Leader, has based his whole argument on what he says is the official record of the debates of the House. From what he is saying, it appears that all he is talking


about are what are commonly known as the "blues". I submit, Mr. Speaker, and it is very clearly established, that the "blues" are not the official record or report of debates. Citation 155.(1) on page 48 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition reads:
The Official Report of Debates, commonly referred to as Hansard, is the record of speeches made in the House; it also contains answers to written questions on the Order Paper.
1 submit that what the Government House Leader is using as a basis for his argument is not the official report of debates. In fact. Citation 156 at page 49 of Beauchesne's says:
The Debates are printed in bound volumes from time to time during a session.
I realize I wear glasses, Mr. Speaker, but I did not see any bound volume of debates. If my hon. friend is basing his argument on what is commonly known as the "blues", his argument must fail.
I would like to make one other point, Mr. Speaker. It is very clear that when the Deputy Speaker occupies the Chair, he has the full authority to exercise all the same powers with respect to decision making as the Speaker himself. This is confirmed by Beauchesne's citing the Speaker of the House of Commons Act, Section 5. It reads:
Every act done and warrant, order or other document issued or published by the Deputy Speaker in relation to any proceedings of the House of Commons, or which under any statute would be done, shall have the same effect and validity as if the same had been done, issued, signed or published by the Speaker for the time being.
By way of conclusion, I would like to say that at this point there is no way that the representatives of the Government can impugn a decision of the Deputy Speaker by implying that in some way it has less force and effect than a ruling made by yourself. The ruling was made by the Deputy Speaker exercising, quite properly, the full authority of the Speaker. That ruling cannot be impugned by any of the interesting, but I must say with all due respect, ineffectual and weak arguments of the Government House Leader and his colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to contribute to the debate on Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, and Motion Nos. 27, 30 and 67 which are presently before the House. This is my first speech before this Chamber, and I would like to take a moment to offer a few of my personal thoughts on the vitally important issue of investment in Canada.
Investment Canada Act
As a new Member of Parliament from Alberta, 1 came to the House determined to voice the views of my constituents and all the people of Alberta. As a small businessman in Edmonton, I witnessed the devastating and discriminating policies of the previous Government. During my 31 years of small business, I witnessed the province grow into an industrial power. I saw Alberta develop. With that development, I understood and shared the positive entrepreneurial attitude of Albertans.
When, following his return to office, Pierre Trudeau said, "Welcome to the 1980s", Albertans suffered the coldest shower in Canadian economic history in the name of Canadi-anization. To many Albertans, Mr. Trudeau's scheme of Canadianization turned out to be a lesson in isolation. When the Opposition talks about-
Mr. Speaker I have a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, 1 respect the fact that this is the first speech of the Hon. Member, but there is a rule of relevance on report stage. We are dealing with an amendment dealing with the extension of time to 45 days from 30 days. It has nothing to do with what Mr. Trudeau said when he came to office in 1980. I would ask that the Hon. Member address himself to the specific amendment before the House at report stage. If he wants to engage in a larger debate on principle, he will have that opportunity at third reading. speechtext: The Hon. Member knows that he should be relevant to the topic of the motions. I am sure the Member will do that.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. Canadianization is very important. It is a topic which was brought up by the Hon. Member of the Opposition. It is very important that we should understand this aspect. Confidence is very necessary for us, otherwise no one could invest in Canada. 1 suggest that that is the real meaning behind the motions that were presented. The other is a question of nationalism and interventionism in the economic forces which drive the market-place.
The motion was perhaps presented by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) with good intentions. Canadians recognize that in order to find new markets and create new jobs and a better future for our children, we must seek out capital from all over the world. The Hon. Member's motion dealing with culturally sensitive proposals underestimates the intelligence of the Canadian community. Placing a time delay on investment, as suggested in the amendment, will serve little purpose. We Canadians know the nature of our society. The people of the country, particularly the unemployed, want economic renewal. I believe that we know how to protect and enhance our own Canadian cultural institutions.


Investment Canada Act
What we need are jobs and this legislation will accomplish that goal.
The amendment to extend review of investment in culturally sensitive activities to 45 days from 30 days is not necessary whatsoever. Our Government promises speed of review that is combined with efficiency. Our Government, in the short time we have been in power, has enacted more good and absolutely necessary legislation than has the previous Government. Of course, it did so after consultation with interested and affected parties.
We are prepared to be more effective and progressively decisive. Investors should not be confused. They will have more confidence in the Government.
I believe that the amendments are not necessary. They are not supported by the Government or the people of Canada, and I strongly suggest that the amendments, particularly Motion No. 67, not pass. We cannot survive in isolation. We cannot live in a cocoon, shielded from the rest of the world. We have an obligation to future generations to build on our strengths and this Bill will provide us with that opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to Motion No. 27 in particular because it concerns new investment in Canada. The proposed amendment would prevent the investment of new funds in new businesses in Canada and it would particularly inhibit the concept of this Bill, which is to develop our nation and to provide work and other opportunities for our children.
Although there is chronic unemployment in our nation, the New Democratic Party has moved an amendment that would require a review of new investment in Canada by some board.
That is not what it says.

Such an amendment would obstruct new and innovative people from coming to our country to create businesses. It is our responsibility to give what Canadians demanded of us on September 4. We must turn the country around and create the opportunities for men and women to work and build this nation. New investment from whatever source is important to provide the opportunity to create.
The New Democrats believe that bureaucrats in Ottawa should decide what investment is acceptable, what jobs people should have, and who should have them. The concept behind this amendment is based on the concept in every slave state where those in power direct their citizens where to work and what to do. They decide on what investment and what technology can be accepted.
Canada has put up with that kind of control for too long. It was that concept which inspired the Foreign Investment Review Act that is now being changed. It was a concept based on the assumption that the bureaucrats in Ottawa who belonged to socialist-oriented parties knew best how development should take place in Canada and how people should use their talents; what should be created and by whom.
That concept was soundly rejected on September 4. This amendment would prevent investment in Canada unless approved by a board of review. There are many type of investment that come to our country. Recently, a new Canadian in my riding had an opportunity to bring a new plastic-fabricating operation to Canada from the United States. His American contact wanted to own a good part of the business because he was supplying the money and the technology. My constituent was primarily supplying the marketing ability.
The lawyer advised the American contact of the Foreign Investment Review Act. That term alone caused the deal to fall through, until I was able to persuade the American investor that the Act was going to be changed so that new investment would be welcome in Canada.
If this amendment is allowed to pass, we would be indicating that new investment is not welcome unless permitted. In some cases, FIRA required investors to spend up to $30,000 to hire lawyers, accountants and others to process the forms that were required for permission to invest in Canada. We are saying, "Come to Canada and invest. Create jobs and opportunities and let us, together, build this country".
