speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I just want to make sure that the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) understands that an affirmative vote-and I am reading from your ruling, Sir, of April 23-on Motion No. 34 disposes of Motion No. 35. A negatived vote on Motion No. 34 necessitates that the question be put on Motion No. 35. If that is clear, then we can proceed with debate, but I want the Hon. Member to understand that so he will not say yea when he means nay or nay when he means yea.

Mr. Speaker, this set of amendments focus on one of the most important clauses in the Bill. It is the area of legislation that describes what form of foreign investment is subject to review. It has been the judgment of the Government obviously that the thresholds should be changed substantially from the way in which they were constructed under the F1RA legislation.
The Government has done this by way of saying, "We want to clarify and simplify matters". At the same time, Mr. Speaker, what the Government has also brought forward by this change in threshold is a major invitation to create a vulnerability for a number of Canadian companies that would be subject, particularly in the case of indirect acquisition, to takeovers that were not constructed with any positive purpose in mind but were done, in large part, because of the manipulation and shenanigans in the New York stock market, the


Investment Canada Act
"team boom pickins" kind of activity that takes place where the stock market becomes a great big game and is simply a matter of rating and pirating various forms of acquisition. In this case, you pick up a lot of Canadian holdings by automatic and inadvertent exercise of that form of high finance pirateer-ing. As a result, Canadian companies that have been well established in Canada that provide useful jobs and economic activity can be wiped out in a flash.
By creating the threshold of indirect acquisitions at the $50 million level a whole range of Canadian subsidiaries now held by parent companies, which includes a very large number of substantially middle-sized companies, will be rolled in as part of the over-all take-up of an indirect acquisition. Canadian communities and workers will be subject to the vagaries and vicissitudes of that activity without having any opportunity for their Government to say whether it is useful, positive and of benefit to Canadians.
We introduced this series of amendments to alter the threshold relationship to make the indirect acquisition threshold the same as the direct acquisition, namely, the $5 million level.
Let me refer to the presentation before the committee of the Science Council, which has a direct mandate to look at how we in Canada can create competitive companies to deal in the international market, particularly in scientific or research related industries. If you look at the testimony of that Council based upon years of researh and years of examination, it shows that the present level of threshold will result in a number of high-tech based companies in Canada being wiped out or taken over without any opportunities for judgment or review by this Government.
Once again we go back to the basic argument we have made. There is nothing wrong with foreign investment as long as foreign investment produces something valuable for Canada, as long as it has the kind of job creation we all want and the kind of investment in new high technology products, with the ability to develop export markets. We have seen time and time again, and the evidence points it out, that many foreign-owned subsidiairies have far less investment in research and development and they prevent Canadian-based subsidiaries from competing with the home corporation in the export market. In other words, they do not provide the kind of performance and behaviour that we need if we are going to build an effective international advantage for Canada.
All we are saying is that companies should at least be required to demonstrate whether they are prepared to make that kind of commitment. We propose that the threshold be brought down so that it can include Canadian subsidiaries acquired in indirect forms. I fail to see why the Government has made such a major discrimination between a direct acquisition and an indirect acquisition. In fact, one could almost argue that it is more important to review indirect acquisitions than direct ones, the reason being that if foreign investors come into Canada to buy Canadian companies and know the performance, attributes and characteristics of those
companies, they are less likely to tamper with or strip them down. However, if they are simply picking up Canadian companies as part of indirect acquisitions as a result of their moving, shaking and manipulating in the financial markets of another company, it does not matter whether the acquisitions are indirect ones. We have seen callousness and indifference toward indirect acquisitions by many of their own companies.
I return to my original point. Perhaps the most flagrant and at times amusing form of financial gymnastics in the United States market is this incredible shotgunning of one company after another. There is a whole new category of stock market sharks who are simply out there to try to boost up stock percentages and dividends in the American market by buying and selling companies at will. Unfortunately, the after effect or side effect is that many Canadian companies are swept up in the rush.
What will happen when the level under this Act is raised to $50 million? Suddenly an investor will look at his sheet of acquisitions and ask how he acquired a company in Pickering, in Moose Jaw or in Corner Brook. What does he know about them? Does he care about Corner Brook or Mississauga? He may say: "Let's get rid of it, sell it off, I don't care". There is no direct involvement on the part of investors in that kind of acquisition.
We have brought forth this set of amendments to ensure that the Government would at least be required to review. This does not mean to say that the Government would be required to stop foreign investment. A fallacy which has been perpetrated time and time again in this debate is that somehow the Foreign Investment Review Act stopped foreign investment. Last year it allowed $4 billion worth of foreign investment into the country, one of the largest allotments of foreign investment in the last 10 years. However, by the review procedure, it required foreign investment coming into the country to demonstrate at least that it had value to Canadians, that it would create jobs and that it would create export markets, not simply be an afterthought or or a side effect.
In coming to grips with these threshold questions, we are really coming to the very heart of our concern that by having the threshold so high, particularly in the area of indirect acquisitions, a number of takeovers will occur which will work to the detriment of many communities, and a number of victims, mainly workers in the companies, will have no recourse. There will be no responsibility or obligation on the part of the Government of Canada to protect their interest.
Those are the reasons that we make the case, once again, that our amendments are designed to improve the Bill and to make it more useful and constructive. They are not in any way designed to detract from the proper procedure or from foreign investment producing something valuable. We believe they will ensure that the review procedure is applied in a way which will make the commitments clear and defined so as to require foreign investment to show the value for Canadians, not simply be allowed to take over companies without demonstrating a major contribution which will be of benefit to Canada.


Whether by inadvertence or not, the Government is at least showing a small flicker of insight and response by allowing certain amendments to take place. Once again, if it were to show another act of inadvertence, this amendment would be the ideal one on which to show it.

Mr. Speaker, with this particular group of amendments, we come to one of the key differences which, frankly, has divided us in our debates on the Investment Canada Bill since it came before the House, in our discussions in committee, and in our attempts at report stage to dig into the substance of the Bill. We have accepted that the Government believes it is in the best interests of Canada to permit new foreign companies to come into the country, to establish new premises or new enterprises and hopefully, to produce jobs, exports and benefits for Canada. This particular set of amendments does not deal with that point of principle. However, there is a second point of principle which we feel is an important one-should we permit small Canadian enterprises, small businesses which are so important to invidual Canadian communities, to be taken over without the review process being brought to bear?
Many Conservative back-benchers have claimed to believe during the debate on the Budget that the small business sector is crucial to our economic future. I believe that strongly, on the basis of my own constituency wherein small business is a vital, vibrant and growing part of the economy, and on the basis of the small business people we met across the country during our action group tour. A tremendous, exciting dynamism exists among small firms throughout the land.
This is a government Bill, and the Government says with this Bill that it believes large Canadian corporations need the safeguard of a review process if there are takeovers from outside the country of medium-sized and large firms. If it is correct in believing that, and if at the same time it is correct in believing that small businesses are crucial to our economic future, then it is equally correct to say that foreign takeovers of small Canadians firms, which are so crucial to us, also deserve to be reviewed. I am not saying that they need to be rejected, because this is not a Bill which rejects foreign investment. It is a Bill which attempts to review foreign investment to see to it that significant benefits come to the country. If there is any sense of honesty in that purpose, if there is any sense of reality in that commitment, I urge government Members to see to it that the review process applies equally to the takeover of small Canadian firms as it does to the takeover of large Canadian firms.
I want to put before the House some of the evidence which makes it crucial for such provisions to be part of the new Act. For instance, let me present the case of Canadian Porcelain, a small enterprise with assets of just over $1 million, based in Hamilton. In the past that enterprise provided insulation mechanisms which were quite significant within the electrical industry. It was forced into receivership by the predatory dumping of its competitors. However, the affected workers got together with the community of Hamilton and discovered that the community was prepared to back them in an excited and
Investment Canada Act
committed way. They brought forward a proposal to take over this bankrupt company and operate it successfully as a workers' co-operative. However, at the last minute, one of the U.S. competitors which had forced Canadian Porcelain into bankruptcy came in and bought up the plant instead. Fortunately,-and I say fortunately because it is as a result of the delay which we have been able to create with respect to the passage of this Bill-the Foreign Investment Review Agency is still the law of the land. Canadian Porcelain workers will be coming to Ottawa on Thursday to meet with the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), and others, to make the case that FIR A should turn down the takeover by Lapp and permit Canadian Porcelain, with its strong base of community support, to keep the industry Canadian.
I would now like to talk about something which is close to the hearts of many of my constituents, that is, the Windsor Spitfires hockey team, which was taken over last year by a Michigan-based enterprise. It is a small operation involving approximately $1 million to $1.5 million in assets, which would not be subject to review under the terms of the Bill before us. Yet the take-over was subject to review by F1RA. That agency saw that the investment was not stopped. Quite frankly, the hockey team needed fresh capital to keep it going. FIR A was able to see to it that a clear commitment was given by the company taking over the team. That commitment involved keeping the team in Windsor and seeing to it that it would continue to employ Canadians, in terms of both its coaching and its support staff. This was something which was absolutely crucial to hockey fans and, indeed, sport fans more widely within my community.
It is possible to go on, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Association for the Advancement of Technology has made the case to the Government that it is the small high-tech firms which will be particularly susceptible to take over if this Bill passes as written. The association has made strong arguments to the Minister. In fact, we heard testimony in committee that the limits in the Bill should be brought down in order that small Canadian high-tech firms could not be taken over without at least a review process taking place. These small high-tech firms are absolutely crucial to our economic future. Bringing down the limits would permit the workers and shareholding partners in some of these firms to have a sense of protection in terms of their interest and their future.
We have also seen what are perhaps the most tragic cases of all in this country. I am speaking of cases where branch plants of U.S. companies are taken over by other huge corporations in the United States, or elsewhere in the world. These large multinational enterprises come to the conclusion, as indeed multinational enterprises must since they are profit-making enterprises, to shut down what now exists as duplicate facilities within their operations. We saw the case in Barrie where the Black & Decker plant was shut down. That shut-down cost 600 workers their jobs. There is absolutely nothing in the Bill before us which will protect Canadian workers employed in small and medium-sized firms which are taken over by the


Investment Canada Act
great conglomerates of the world and which are subject to rationalization and some type of global profit maximization strategy.
I make the case to the House that if we accept the amendment before us, we will bring to bear a review process-not a harsh one but a significant one-to protect the interests of workers in communities with respect to small Canadian branch plants which will be subject, in the future, to the pressures of world capitalism as it rationalizes throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, l wish to comment with respect to Motion No. 34. In my view, this motion appears to deal with what I find to be the most despicable portion of the Foreign Investment Review Act. I am speaking of what happened when a Canadian subsidiary of a multinational company was transferred by one multinational to another in a world transaction made outside Canada. What happens is that a multinational may have a Canadian corporation as one of its many companies. The effect of transferring the control of the multinational involves, in effect, the transfer of the control of the Canadian corporation. Under the provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act, the bureaucrats in Ottawa were expected to make a ruling as to whether or not one multinational company could take over the assets of another involving transactions of many millions of dollars. Indeed, in some cases, billions of dollars have been involved. These transactions took place in world-held corporations because one small entity involved in that conglomerate happened to exist in Canada. In some cases, in order to avoid the question of review, the Canadian subsidiary has been closed down completely. The thinking seemed to be, "Why bother trying to appease these people in Canada who think they know better than anyone else with respect to investment and how to create jobs?"
More important, the whole aspect of the Foreign Investment Review Act, as it operated in this sense, called into question the nature of Canada as a place to invest money and do business. This seriously hampered the investment of funds and the number of job opportunities for Canadians, perhaps in the most gross manner possible. The mover of the amendment which I am now discussing wishes to reinstate this concept if the assets of a company involve more than $5 million. Surely to goodness we are part of an international trading and development system. Some of our multinational companies are the largest multinational companies in the world. In the distilling industry alone, we have the top two distillers in the world, Joseph E. Seagram & Sons Limited and Hiram Walker & Sons Limited, number one and number two respectively. Our multinational corporations are able to deal, grow and do business. That we should say to another country's multinational, which may happen to have a branch operation somewhere in Canada that has nothing to do with the totality of its world-wide organization, that its world-wide activities are to be reviewed simply because of its operation in Canada, then we go a long way toward hurting Canada and the concept of Canada as a place where fair and free trade and open business are conducted.
The philosophy expressed by the Opposition seems to be that somehow the public officials know better than the business community how investment is to take place and how it is made. As a result of the attitudes in the Foreign Investment Review Act which tried to review transactions that did not take place in Canada at all and tried to review transactions for which the essence of the transactions were not Canadian at all, we have called into question the whole nature of investment in Canada. Canada is not deemed to be a fair place to put money because one cannot assign what one owns in Canada to someone else. Those kinds of transactions do not involve further foreign investment in Canada and never involved that at all. They do not involve a new takeover in Canada. They are only a matter of whether or not a multinational corporation with headquarters in Holland would take over the activities of a multinational corporation with headquarters in New York. What difference does that make to us? It is still a foreign-owned corporation. It is still part of a conglomerate.
In the view of this Government, we want to let members of the investment world know that Canada is a place to do business. We want to let them know that if they invest their assets in this country, they can sell them to whomever they wish. There are certain limitations on that and those limitations are spelled out in the Bill. They involve cultural matters and things that go to the essence of Canadianism. However, in terms of ordinary commercial activities, surely to goodness transactions of this nature should not be reviewed.

Motion No. 38A
That Bill C-15, be amended in Clause 14 by adding immediately after line 15 at page 10 the following:
"(e) gross assets shall be determined as at the latest completed fiscal period at
current prices in a manner prescribed by regulations."
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is striking that one of the key considerations within this Bill is the size of a given investment. There are threshold levels which set out trigger points which determine whether or not an investment will be reviewed. Yet we do not at any stage talk about how we will measure those trigger points.
This is partly a technical point and partly a substantive point. In our view, if it is not set out clearly within the Bill the way in which a trigger mechanism will be used, there is a serious danger that we could have a system in place whereby the way in which gross assets are measured for purposes of the
Investment Canada Act
trigger mechanism will grossly undervalue those assets. That of course would mean that takeovers that should be reviewable according to the intent of the legislation would not be reviewable because the way their asset levels are calculated leaves them under the triggering level.
The triggering level itself is $5 million in the case of a direct acquisition and $50 million in the case of an indirect acquisition. As Members of the House who are in business or who have a background in law or economics will know, many different conventions are taken to establish what constitutes the assets of a company. For instance, it is possible to look at the $5 million threshold on the basis of historical costs as depreciated within a company. On that basis, a person might easily have a company which, at fair market value, is worth $20 million, however, on its books, with historical values depreciated, it would be worth approximately $3 million. That would mean that a company which should be reviewed would escape review. Therefore, we have brought before the House a technical amendment which is designed to ensure that the substantive purpose of the Bill is achieved. The amendment states:
-gross assets shall be determined as at the latest completed fiscal period at current prices in a manner prescribed by regulations.
In short, we are attempting to have a value placed on assets which reflect a fair market value of the assets, rather than an artificial level which would arise from bookkeeping conventions and the operation of depreciation over a long period of time.
With respect to family-owned businesses, this is a particularly important amendment. As many Members will be aware, most family-owned businesses do not offer shares on the public stock market. Their books are likely to be calculated on the basis of historical costs and assets, and there is likely to be a depreciation charged against those historical costs in order to reach a nominal book value level. If we do not do something to ensure directly within the legislation that there is a definition of asset value which represents fair market value, then family businesses in particular will likely be taken over without the review process.
I would be particularly interested in hearing comments on this amendment from my Conservative colleagues who have experience in the accounting profession. 1 would like to make the point that this is an attempt to ensure that the stated purpose of the Bill, as brought forward by the Minister-that is to say, that companies with an asset value higher thant $5 million will be reviewed-will in practice be respected.

Mr. Speaker, I was particularly impressed with the fact that the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), in his description of the types of companies which he would want to be scourged by the amendment, would name family businesses. He said it would be those family businesses which do not keep proper records that would have to be inspected and re-audited in order to have some indication of the current value of the assets. His


Investment Canada Act
attitude is that family businesses are the businesses which should be hounded by the amendment which he has proposed. Is that not typical of the New Democratic Party, to ensure that family businesses are the businesses which should have to go to some sort of re-evaluation and produce some sort of a new current eveluation system demanded in the statute with respect to determining whether their gross asset value is within in the purview of the statute?
The present contemplation of the Bill is that what is a gross asset will be defined in the regulations. That is the kind of thing which is normally left to regulations. I do not believe that any of us is really happy about regulations, but it is possible and easy to change regulations with respect to "gross assets", which is a technical term, and do that, if it does not work out, in a way which will be different as time and experience indicate.
He said that the legislation should state: "the latest completed fiscal period". What is the latest completed fiscal period? Presumably, it is the last year end of the company. So if the company is sold ten months after the year end, presumably we would have to go back to the latest fiscal period. The motion also states, "Current prices". When are the prices current? Are they current at the last fiscal period, or are they the current prices when the sale takes place? Is that not a wonderful thing for an accountant or a lawyer to interfere with or to understand? That is the very reason for which these things are done by regulations.
The amendment which was produced by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor is one which does not add much other than complications and problems to the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I rise briefly to indicate that we support the amendment which was brought forward by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). We believe it to be a very useful clarification of how to compute gross assets. Once again I will turn to the case which we have tried to make time and again in the House, that if the purpose of Investment Canada is to simplify and facilitate the process, that means the business community must have a higher level of certainty about what to expect. If the present Bill is left intact, as it was originally contrived, it could lead to all sorts of what might politely be called creative accounting principles in order that companies could get below the threshold levels. But by establishing clearly in the statute the formula by which those assets would be computed, that uncertainty would be eliminated. It would ensure that there would be no attempt to become manipulative or creative in determining what the assets would be.
I find it exceedingly strange that the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who has been the great crusader against over-regulation in Government, is now defending it. What a difference several months makes in terms of one's principles. How quickly they change.
The fact of the matter is that it is not a useful idea always to put things in regulation. It is better, if possible, to put them in statutory requirements, which are passed by Parliament, to
have them entrenched in the legislation. That is exactly what this amendment intends to do. It intends to clarify the matter.
We think that the amendment is proper and we will support
it.

Motion No. 41
That Bill C-15, be amended in Clause 15 by striking out lines 9 to 13 at page 11 and substituting the following therefor:
"(a) it falls within a prescribed type of business that is related to Canada's cultural heritage or national identity including the publication, distribution or sale of books, magazines, periodicals or newspapers in print or machine-readable form; the production, distribution, sale or exhibition of film or video products; the production, distribution, sale or exhibition of audio or video music recordings; the publication, distribution or sale of music in print or machine-readable form; the production, distribution or sale of educational materials, or other such businesses to be further specified in regulations pursuant to this Act; and".
He said: Mr. Speaker, when debate was introduced in this House on second reading, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) extended an invitation to this House. He said, "We believe there should be full and active review in the area of cultural heritage and national identity". He said, "I want this House to help me find that concept. I want to ensure that those areas which are most vulnerable and sensitive to foreign takeovers would be adequately protected by Parliament".


During committee we spent a great deal of time looking at that concept. We had a number of very useful presentations put before us by book publishers and various different cultural organizations. They came forward with what we believe to be a very useful and important way in which Parliament itself could clearly put its statement on what it believes to be an adequate protection for national identity and cultural heritage. But once again, Mr. Speaker, the Government has changed its mind. Once again the Minister's words are not worth the paper they are written on. We might as well throw Hansard out, because when we come to introducing an amendment which would entrench in the statutes those areas of our cultural heritage and national identity which need protection, the Minister refuses it. He says he will leave it up to regulation, which can be rewritten at a moment's notice by Order in Council. It can be stuck away in the Gazette somewhere, and it means that all those organizations out there which were looking for some degree of guarantee and assurance will be denied that opportunity. That shows the total disdain this Minister has. We have seen it today. He has not been in the House during the report stage, the most important part of the debate on any Minister's Bill. Where is he, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Without reflecting on the Hon. Member's presence in the House, I draw to his attention that it is not parliamentary to reflect upon the absence of other Hon. Members in the House. I would welcome it if the Hon. Member would return to the address which he was creating in the lobby.

Mr. Speaker, I would be more than happy to continue even though there are certain critical and strategic individuals and personalities who should be here but who are not, but I would not think of naming them.
With respect to this amendment, Mr. Speaker, the point is that this seems to be a right of Parliament. The Minister gave us the invitation which he is now ignoring. He does not want to deal with it. I know the reason why. It is because the Government really has no intention of living up to the protection and guarantee of those crucial industries.
In the last six to seven months there have been a number of important cases dealing with book publishing before the Government, with which it could easily dispense, which would provide a very clear signal to foreign investors that in crucial strategic areas we do not want foreign purchases. Yet because of the lack of attention and decision by the Minister, we now have even further takeovers. A number of new takeovers were announced in April and May by other foreign investors in the book publishing industry. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister is really not vitally interested in having any kind
Investment Canada Act
of control or restriction of foreign investment in the cultural area.
I would like to draw to the attention of the House another important and crucial area. Sometimes we have to laugh at the pretensions of this Government. It says it is the Government of the new social order. It is going to be in the vanguard of change. We had a number of people before the committee who said, "Look. The world is changing and data processing is the one area which it is crucial to protect". It is the 1980s equivalent of book publishing. People now put all kinds of things on computers. There is all kinds of software. What the computer people are saying is that there is an enormous haemorrhage of computer data processing to the United States. Close to $2 billion or $3 billion is lost every year in that industry simply because at this point in time there is no protection. Therefore, we introduced that responsibility in the amendment. We are saying, "Let's incorporate that as part of our cultural heritage and make sure that it is protected by legislation". Is the pioneer of change, the Government which is in the vanguard of the new electronic age, prepared to recognize that? No, it does not even deal with the matter. It will not even consider it. It will not give Parliament the right to make its voice heard by ensuring that it is part of the legislation. What that really adds up to, Mr. Speaker, is a subterfuge, a camouflage. This Government has no intention of providing protection for the cultural industries. It has very little interest in national identity. It does not want to have Parliament speak with a voice which will allow for that protection.
In this last moment before we start the vote, it would seem to me that those Hon. Members who listen to their conscience and feel that it is important that Parliament retain its rightful role to speak for the Canadian people and to protect our Canadian cultural and national identity, would vote for this amendment.
